title: Verifier‑Assisted versus LLM‑Only Pre‑deployment Network‑Change Validation: A Preregistered Paired Study
abstract: We measured whether adding a deterministic pre‑deployment verifier plus a bounded automated repair budget increases the fraction of intent‑driven network‑change proposals that pass semantic validation compared with accepting a single LLM candidate. Under a preregistered paired design (study id cnsmp2026-llm-verifier-predeployment-001) we executed 300 paired intents (100 per difficulty stratum) using gpt-5-mini and deterministic_netops_validator_v5. Each paired intent produced one shared_initial candidate reused for both conditions: baseline (accept single shot) and guarded (validator + ≤1 automated repair). Results: baseline 299/300 unflagged passes (0.9966667), guarded 300/300 (1.0); contingency n11=299, n10=1, n01=0, n00=0; absolute paired difference = 0.0033333; exact two‑sided McNemar p = 1.0; 95% paired bootstrap percentile CI = [0.00, 0.01] (bootstrap_seed = 1729, B = 10000). The single deterministic rescue required one repair invocation across 300 pairs (model_calls_used = 301). We archive the preregistration and execution artifacts; we interpret findings with respect to estimand conditioning (shared_initial), ceiling effects, validator coverage, and repair‑budget constraints.

sections.introduction: Generative large language models (LLMs) are increasingly proposed for NetOps tasks such as intent→configuration translation, template synthesis, and automated repair. For pre‑deployment network changes, operational safety requires semantic correctness (sequencing constraints, reachability, policy preservation) that syntactic checks alone do not guarantee. A common engineering approach pairs generative models with deterministic validators and bounded automated repair (generate→validate→repair) to reduce deployment risk. Prior work has shown that tool augmentation and validation can improve correctness, but reported gains depend on (i) whether evaluations permit resampling or verifier‑guided regeneration, (ii) the validator's expressiveness, and (iii) the allowed repair budget. To bound the deterministic rescue attributable to post‑generation checking alone, we preregistered a paired experiment that conditions on a single shared LLM draw per intent and compares accepting that single candidate versus running a deterministic validator with at most one automated repair. The primary research question: does adding a deterministic verifier plus ≤1 automated repair increase the probability that a single LLM candidate passes semantic pre‑deployment validation compared with accepting that same candidate without repair?
sections.related_work: Recent surveys and system papers document a broad set of LLM applications for NetOps and emphasize tooling tradeoffs: intent translation, configuration synthesis, protocol test generation, and automated repair [1–6]. Tool‑augmented architectures (planner‑centric frameworks, ReAct‑style pipelines) enable LLMs to call external validators and decomposers to handle multi‑step workflows [2,7]. Empirical reports indicate that generate→validate→repair scaffolds can improve surface correctness metrics compared with unconstrained generation, but magnitudes vary with task distribution and validator coverage [3,4]. Methodologically, prior evaluations often conflate deterministic validation benefits with resampling or iterative regeneration; disentangling these sources requires explicit estimand choices. Finally, multiple works argue for semantic benchmarks and verifiers that capture sequencing and reachability invariants rather than only syntactic template correctness [5,8]. Our study explicitly isolates the bounded deterministic‑repair effect by holding the LLM draw fixed across conditions, aligning evaluation with deployment policies that limit additional model calls.
sections.methodology:
Preregistration and estimand. We preregistered the confirmatory design (study id cnsmp2026-llm-verifier-predeployment-001; preregistration SHA‑256 archived) and fixed the primary estimand: the absolute paired difference in the unflagged verifier‑pass proportion (guarded − baseline) on N = 300 paired intents after applying prespecified inclusion/exclusion rules. The preregistration specified a paired analysis executor, multiplicity handling for exploratory strata tests, a bounded repair budget (≤1 automated repair), and deterministic scoring rules.

Task suite and stratification. Tasks were deterministically generated into a synthetic topology suite stratified into low/medium/high difficulty (100 pairs per stratum). Each task encodes (i) a natural‑language intent, (ii) initial and expected final device states, (iii) sequencing constraints (e.g., must_be_down_for_fields), (iv) preservation invariants, and (v) protected interfaces. Difficulty metadata (changed_interface_count, dependency_rule_count, required_command_count) determined stratum assignment.

Shared_initial protocol, model, and configuration. To isolate deterministic rescue from resampling benefits we implemented a shared_initial estimand: for each pair a single LLM candidate was generated and reused verbatim for both baseline and guarded conditions. The declared generator was gpt-5-mini; generation parameters and adapter settings were fixed before execution. Reuse of the same candidate prevents any advantage from additional independent model draws and measures only the deterministic validator and bounded repair effect applied to an identical output.

Validator, scoring, and repair operator. Semantic evaluation used deterministic_netops_validator_v5 implementing a full_intent_constraint_validation rule that deterministically checks sequencing invariants, required command patterns, preservation of unspecified state, topology reachability invariants encoded by the synthetic suite, and forbidden‑template protections. Scoring was binary (unflagged = pass). The guarded pipeline permitted at most one automated repair attempt. The repair operator is a constrained edit routine limited to localized sequencing and insertion edits (for example, inserting a missing 'admin down' before a VLAN or MTU change). Repairs were applied only to flagged candidates and were re‑validated deterministically; repaired candidates that remained flagged counted as guarded failures in the primary analysis.

Contamination controls, missingness rules, and stopping rule. The preregistration included negative controls and deterministic contamination checks. A pair would be excluded from confirmatory analysis only if both pipeline calls for that pair failed due to provider/infrastructure outage; single‑call failures were handled per the executor's complete‑pair policy with planned sensitivity analyses. The stopping rule required halting if >20% of attempted pairs were excluded due to dual‑call outages. These rules were fixed prior to observing outcomes.
sections.results:
Execution integrity. The registered adapter completed the confirmatory run with 600 completed episodes producing 300 paired observations under the shared_initial protocol. Execution summary: planned_episode_count = 600, completed_episode_count = 600, complete_pair_count = 300, model_calls_used = 301. Stage accounting showed 300 shared_initial generations and a single repair invocation; no provider/infrastructure outages occurred and no pairs were excluded.

Primary outcomes. Binary scoring produced baseline_success_count = 299 and guarded_success_count = 300 (baseline = 299/300 = 0.9966667; guarded = 300/300 = 1.0). The paired contingency counts were n11 = 299, n10 = 1, n01 = 0, n00 = 0. The absolute paired difference (guarded − baseline) = 0.0033333. The preregistered exact two‑sided McNemar test (operating on discordant counts n10 and n01) returned p = 1.0. A paired bootstrap percentile 95% confidence interval computed with seed = 1729 and B = 10000 yields [0.00, 0.01]. Because discordance is minimal (m = 1), the exact test has limited sensitivity; the bootstrap CI bounds plausible absolute improvement to at most one percentage point in this context.

Per‑stratum diagnostics and repair trace. Per stratum tallies were: low baseline 100/100 and guarded 100/100; medium baseline 100/100 and guarded 100/100; high baseline 99/100 and guarded 100/100. The solitary discordant pair occurred in the high stratum and invoked the permitted automated repair: the validator initially flagged a sequencing omission (missing 'admin down' before a VLAN/MTU change). The constrained repair inserted the missing sequencing command and the validator reported the corrected candidate as valid. That single repair produced the only deterministic rescue observed.

Cost and operational footprint. The guarded pipeline required one additional repair stage call across 300 pairs (model_calls_used = 301), indicating a negligible marginal model‑call cost for the deterministic rescue observed under the chosen repair operator and task suite.

Missingness and contamination. Contamination checks and negative controls produced no unexpected passes; the missingness summary reports zero failed or unscorable episodes and zero excluded pairs under the preregistered rules.
sections.discussion:
Interpretation relative to operational estimands. The shared_initial estimand conditions on a single generator draw per intent and therefore matches deployment policies that tightly limit model calls for cost, latency, or governance reasons. Under such policies the guarded pipeline measures only deterministic validation and bounded repair applied to the same candidate. Evaluations that permit resampling, interactive verifier‑guided regeneration, or iterative repair address a different estimand and will generally show larger achievable success rates by exploiting generator variance.

Ceiling effects and pilot omission. The preregistration planned an optional pilot (n = 60) to estimate discordance for power calibration; that pilot was not executed. Consequently the main run confronted a near‑ceiling baseline (299/300), producing minimal discordance (m = 1) and limited power to detect small absolute differences. This outcome illustrates the practical benefit of small calibration pilots when single‑shot generator performance may approach ceiling on a chosen suite.

Validator coverage and failure‑mode dependence. The single observed failure was a sequencing omission; other failure classes (reachability violations, ACL removal) were rare or absent in this synthetic suite. The marginal value of a guarded pipeline therefore depends on (i) the distribution of failure modes in deployment and (ii) validator expressiveness: richer validators that capture deeper reachability or policy semantics may increase rescue rates, while narrower validators yield correspondingly smaller measurable benefits.

Repair budget tradeoffs. We intentionally limited automated repair to a single constrained edit to quantify bounded deterministic rescue. Iterative or more permissive repair operators, or verifier‑guided regeneration, would measure different operational tradeoffs (higher rescue potential at the cost of extra model calls and complexity). The archived repair trace for the rescued episode can inform design choices for permitted edit operators in production pipelines.

Practical implications for NetOps CI/CD. Organizations should align evaluation estimands with operational constraints. If model calls are tightly budgeted, the shared_initial estimand gives an operationally meaningful bound on deterministic verifier/repair rescue per single candidate. If pipelines can afford resampling or iterative strategies, evaluations should allow such operations to measure achievable success under those policies. Our run shows that, under the synthetic suite and repair budget used here, deterministic repair produced exactly one rescue at negligible additional model‑call expenditure.
sections.conclusion: In a preregistered paired comparison that conditioned on a single LLM draw per intent (shared_initial) and allowed at most one constrained automated repair, baseline single‑shot generation using gpt-5-mini achieved 299/300 unflagged verifier passes and the guarded pipeline 300/300, yielding an absolute paired improvement of 0.00333 (exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.0; 95% bootstrap CI [0.00,0.01]). The guarded pipeline deterministically rescued one sequencing omission via a single automated repair invocation. Because baseline performance was near ceiling on this synthetic suite, observable deterministic rescue was limited. These artifact‑archived findings bound the deterministic rescue achievable under strict per‑change model‑call budgets and demonstrate how estimator conditioning, validator design, and repair budget jointly determine the operational utility of guarded LLM pipelines. We release the preregistration, execution, and analysis artifacts to support reproducibility and to enable targeted follow‑up work that varies estimand conditioning, model strength, task distribution, or repair budget to explore regimes where guarded rescue is larger or where resampling is permitted.

limitations: Synthetic benchmark: tasks and topologies were generated by the preregistered deterministic generator; real‑world heterogeneity may surface different failure modes and increase validator marginal utility.
Single model and validator: only gpt-5-mini and deterministic_netops_validator_v5 were evaluated; results may not generalize to other LLMs or richer/diverse validators.
Ceiling effect: baseline single‑shot performance was near 100% on this suite (299/300), producing minimal discordance and limited power to detect small absolute improvements.
Pilot not executed: the preregistered calibration pilot for discordance estimation was not run; no post‑preregistration power recalculation was performed.

Estimand conditioning: the shared_initial protocol conditions on a single LLM candidate and therefore does not measure verifier benefits that would arise from allowing independent alternative LLM candidates per condition (resampling or iterative regeneration).
Repair budget: the guarded condition permitted at most one automated repair per pair; larger or iterative repair strategies may yield different outcomes.
